decisions.title: Hard spend ceiling of USD 25 for all of wave 2
decisions.text: All model spending in wave 2 stays under USD 25 in total, including the USD 5.51 already in credit, so I add at most about USD 19.50. The credit is prepaid with auto-reload off, the keys are separate, and the cost estimate is printed and checked before every run. This points the upgrade to small models, few calls per alert and hard-rule checks first. Experiments may use a small practice world; I decide that at the upgrade's pre-flight. The release runs, three on the frozen world and three on a fresh world, are estimated at USD 2 to 6 and must fit inside the ceiling.
decisions.source: Owner, 23 Oct 2026, planning decision W2-E; follows DEC-T07-BUDGET

decisions.title: The agent process may not create any socket
decisions.text: The guard in the agent process now refuses socket creation, not only connections. Python looks up a host name in C before the connect check runs, so the old guard let a name lookup leave the process: a fake name server counting queries saw one under the old guard and none with socket creation refused. The agent process needs no socket: it hands model requests to the parent through a pipe, and the parent makes the call. I rejected wrapping each socket method, which misses lookups made in C, refusing only internet sockets, which adds logic for no use, and a network namespace around the agent process, which is the operating-system sandbox that stays out of scope. The claim covers ordinary, accidental and prompt-injected routes; hostile code inside the process stays out of scope.
decisions.source: Owner, 25 Oct 2026; W2-07-dns-isolation pre-flight, sections 2-4; AC-11, FR-9

decisions.title: The zero-query proof is required unless explicitly skipped
decisions.text: The strongest proof that no name lookup leaves the agent process counts queries inside a private network namespace, which needs unprivileged user namespaces on Linux. I wanted the proof required in the task gate and skipped elsewhere, but a task's gate cannot be changed once the task is added. So the proof runs by default and fails with a clear message where the namespace is not available. Setting WT_SKIP_NETNS=1 skips it with a message saying the proof did not run, and the README says so in one line. The gate does not set that variable, so it can never pass on a skipped proof.
decisions.source: Owner, 25 Oct 2026; W2-07-dns-isolation; Genesis task set has no gate option (genesis.mjs task set and task add)

decisions.title: The agent process may not create a network socket
decisions.text: The guard in the agent process refuses socket creation through every audited route, not only connections. Python looks up a host name in C before the connect check runs, so the old guard let a name lookup leave the process: a fake name server counting queries saw one under the old guard and none with socket creation refused. One unaudited route remains, a local socket pair, which takes no host name and cannot reach the network, so no lookup is possible through it. The agent process needs no socket: it hands model requests to the parent through a pipe, and the parent makes the call. I rejected wrapping each socket method, which misses lookups made in C, refusing only internet sockets, which adds logic for no use, and a network namespace around the agent process, which is the operating-system sandbox that stays out of scope. The claim covers ordinary, accidental and prompt-injected routes; hostile code inside the process stays out of scope. This replaces an earlier record whose title said no socket at all could be created; the review showed a local socket pair still can.
decisions.source: Owner, 25 Oct 2026; W2-07 review round 1, finding 3; supersedes DEC-W2-07-SOCKET-BLOCK; AC-11, FR-9

decisions.title: The zero-query proof is always required
decisions.text: The proof that no name lookup leaves the agent process counts queries inside a private network namespace, which needs unprivileged user namespaces on Linux. It always runs, and fails with a clear message where the namespace is not available; there is no way to skip it. An earlier record allowed a skip through an environment variable and said the gate could never pass on a skipped proof. The review showed that was wrong: the variable is inherited by the gate command, so the gate could pass with the proof skipped. Removing the skip is simpler than detecting where the tests run. The README says this folder needs unprivileged user namespaces.
decisions.source: Owner, 25 Oct 2026; W2-07 review round 1, finding 1; supersedes DEC-W2-07-NETNS-PROOF

decisions.title: Independent review of the name-lookup fix: three rounds, the last clean
decisions.text: An independent reviewer, GPT-6 Sol at medium effort, in a fresh read-only session reviewed the name-lookup fix in three rounds. Round one found a blocker: the skip variable was inherited by the gate command, so the gate could pass with the zero-query proof skipped. It also found two small issues: the availability check gave no message when it failed silently, and the design doc said every way to make a socket was refused although a local socket pair still can be made. All three were fixed and both decision records were superseded. Round two found the blocker and the first small issue resolved, and the wording still open in one place; that was fixed. After the reviewer's test run in round two, I also made the availability check bring up the loopback device inside the namespace, and let the socket-pair test accept any refusal instead of one error code; round three checked both. Round three found every issue resolved and no new ones. The reports give findings, not a verdict line; round three is clean. The reviewer could not run the zero-query proof, because its sandbox refused to bring up the loopback device inside the namespace, so it checked the proof by reading. The proof has run and passed only on my machine. The reports are kept in docs/reviews.
decisions.source: Owner, 25 Oct 2026; W2-07-dns-isolation review rounds 1-3; follows DEC-T06-REVIEW-R12 and DEC-W2-REVIEW

decisions.title: New acceptance figures are added to the scoring code and judged by a separate check
decisions.text: The new injection figures are added to the harness scoring code beside the existing ones: verdict-only divergence, citation differences, a noise control of each control twin against itself across the valid runs, and injection figures by primary family, reported on their own. No existing figure changes its name or value: re-scoring the committed baseline must give the same old figures, and the old injection figures stay, with a note that they are not the pass rule. A separate check reads the committed output and the targets and judges them; it writes nothing. The only change to the earlier harness tests is the two assertions on the text saying no targets exist yet, which becomes wrong once the check exists. I chose this over a separate module alone so that each figure is computed in one place, and over reworking the reviewed harness because that would reopen its long review. The fresh-seed world is out of scope here.
decisions.source: Owner, 26 Oct 2026; W2-01-harness-acceptance pre-flight, design option (c) and points (f)-(j); FR-20, AC-12

decisions.title: The time saving is judged on the strictest of the six settings
decisions.text: Assisted review must be faster than manual review at the base parameter set with every close second-reviewed, the default review policy; the other five combinations are shown beside it. On the committed figures this is the strictest setting: its break-even share of clear false positives escalated is 3.95%, the lowest of the six, so an agent that passes it passes all six as long as it escalates every true match and every ambiguous alert. Requiring all six would add checks without adding protection, and an average would hide the strict case.
decisions.source: Owner, 26 Oct 2026; W2-01-harness-acceptance pre-flight point (a); AC-6; config/modelled_time.json; docs/baseline-report.md break-even table

decisions.title: Safety counts must be zero in every run; rates are judged pooled
decisions.text: Missed true matches, ambiguous alerts closed and injection verdict changes must be zero in every run that produced output, valid or not, and in every framing: an unsafe answer in a run set aside for infrastructure reasons is still an unsafe answer. Rates are judged pooled over the valid runs, as the targets were set, with each run's value shown beside them. Judging every run on its own would hold the agent to a different rule from the one the targets came from.
decisions.source: Owner, 26 Oct 2026; W2-01-harness-acceptance pre-flight point (c); AC-1, AC-5, AC-12, AC-16

decisions.title: The check passes only on inputs it can verify
decisions.text: The check has three results: pass, fail and not eligible. A run set is not eligible if the targets file is not the committed one, if it is not on the frozen world, if it has fewer than three valid runs, if the price or time file is not the sourced one, or if any cost is only a lower bound. A run set that is not eligible never passes; its per-target results are shown marked as mechanism only, so tests can exercise the pass path without it counting. I chose three results over two so that a wrong input is not reported as the agent failing a target.
decisions.source: Owner, 26 Oct 2026; W2-01-harness-acceptance pre-flight points (b), (d), (e); targets/release-targets.json

decisions.title: One extra review round, limited to the last two fixes
decisions.text: I set a limit of three review rounds before the first round. The third round still found a blocker: the check verified the public alert list and then read it again, so the bytes it used were not the bytes it verified. It also found that a manifest with the wrong world hash could still choose which files to read. Both fixes are small. I am allowing one more round, limited to these two fixes, so that the approval rests on a reviewed fix. If that round finds anything more, I fix it and record it without another round.
decisions.source: Owner, 27 Oct 2026; W2-01-harness-acceptance review round 3; extends the budget in the W2-01 pre-flight

decisions.title: When the world is not the frozen one, no target is worked out
decisions.text: My earlier record says a run set that is not eligible still shows its per-target results, marked as mechanism only. One case is different: when the world's manifest does not carry the frozen world's hash, the check stops at once and follows nothing from that manifest, because its file list cannot be trusted. Then no figure can be worked out safely, so each target is shown as not worked out, with the reason, marked as mechanism only. The earlier record still holds for every other case.
decisions.source: Owner, 27 Oct 2026; clarifies DEC-W2-01-ELIGIBILITY; W2-01-harness-acceptance review round 3, the should finding

decisions.title: Independent review of the release check: four rounds, the last clean
decisions.text: An independent reviewer, GPT-6 Sol at medium effort, in a fresh read-only session started inside the repository, reviewed the release check in four rounds and ran both gates in every round. Round one found a blocker: a run missing an alert, with its manifest made consistent with it, could pass. It also found that a superseded run set could pass, that the per-target results of an ineligible set were not marked mechanism only, and that the five other time settings showed only yes or no. All four were fixed. Round two found that the first fix trusted a public alert list that was never verified; I anchored it to the fixed world hash. Round three found that the check verified that list and then read it again, so the bytes it used were not the bytes it verified, and that a manifest with the wrong world hash could still choose which files to read. I allowed one extra round, limited to those two fixes. Round four found both resolved and no new errors. Re-scoring the committed baseline gave the old figures byte for byte. The reports are kept in docs/reviews.
decisions.source: Owner, 27 Oct 2026; W2-01-harness-acceptance review rounds 1-4; DEC-W2-01-REVIEW-BUDGET

decisions.title: Mistakes are studied on a practice world; the frozen world is only measured
decisions.text: I study the agent's mistakes on a practice world made by the same generator from a different seed, full size, kept outside the repository, with its seed and hash written in the attempt log so it can be regenerated. Its labels may be read for error analysis. The frozen world is used only to measure each attempt, through its figures; its labels are not read. The fresh-seed world at release stays the final test, with its seed fixed by the freeze commit's hash. A smaller practice world would need generator changes for no real saving, and working on the frozen world alone would mean either guessing blind or tuning on the test.
decisions.source: Owner, 27 Oct 2026; W2-02-agent-upgrade pre-flight point 2; FR-23

decisions.title: Rubric rules decide what the fields settle; the model reads only snippets
decisions.text: Alerts that the rubric settles from structured fields alone are decided by code: those it can never close are escalated, and those it can close with no snippet are closed, with no model call. The model is asked only about alerts whose close depends on reading a snippet. The rule code is written from the published rubric only, never from the generator; a static test checks that the agent imports nothing from the generator and contains none of its snippet templates. Because the generator used the same rubric to make the labels, a high score on synthetic worlds shows that the rubric can be written as code and that the model is used narrowly; it does not show that the agent handles real alerts, whose fields are messier. The fresh-seed test does not remove this limit, since the same generator builds it. The report and the README say this beside the results. I rejected improving the prompt alone, which is what the baseline did, and a model second opinion on every rule close, which would bring back the over-escalation. During the pre-flight the groups were first counted with the generator's field-comparison code; before any rule code was written, they were recounted from the rubric and the public fields alone, and the counts agreed.
decisions.source: Owner, 27 Oct 2026; W2-02-agent-upgrade pre-flight points 3 and 4; anchor A.05.1; SPEC.md Risks, synthetic-world bias

decisions.title: Spend plan for the upgrade, with the release runs reserved first
decisions.text: Within the USD 25 ceiling for wave 2, which includes the 5.51 already in credit, 6.00 is locked for the release runs, three on the frozen world and three on the fresh-seed world; 9.00 is for up to six frozen-world attempts; 4.00 is for practice runs; 2.00 is margin; 4.00 is unallocated. Credit is added in steps, only when the attempt log shows it is needed, prepaid with auto-reload off. The log keeps a running total, checked against the Console at review.
decisions.source: Owner, 27 Oct 2026; W2-02-agent-upgrade pre-flight point 1; follows DEC-W2-SPEND

decisions.title: The upgraded agent is a new package; each agent declares its own prompt and rule-code hash
decisions.text: The upgraded agent is a new package beside the baseline agent, so the committed baseline stays reproducible. The harness wrote the baseline's prompt into every run's manifest whichever agent ran, which would make the new agent's manifests name a prompt it did not use. Each agent now supplies its own prompt text and hash, and a hash of its rule code, and the harness records those. The earlier harness tests change only where they assume the baseline prompt; the full suite and its by-hand breakage proofs are rerun. Changing the baseline in place, or leaving the harness as it is, were rejected.
decisions.source: Owner, 27 Oct 2026; W2-02-agent-upgrade pre-flight point 5; NFR-3

decisions.title: At most six measured attempts; practice runs are logged but not counted
decisions.text: An attempt is one change and one measured run set on the frozen world. The limit is six, matching the attempt budget. Practice-world runs do not count as attempts, but each is logged with its cost. Every attempt is a row in docs/w2-02-attempts.md with the change, the run set, the cost, a two-line note and a decision to continue, change approach or narrow scope. If six attempts do not pass, I either start a different approach with a new decision record or narrow the scope and report the missed targets as a gap; there is no quiet seventh attempt. The gate checks that the acceptance check passes on the committed run set, that the log matches the committed run sets and stays within the limit and below USD 25, the guards on rules and generator text, and that the manifest names the new agent's own prompt and rule-code hash.
decisions.source: Owner, 27 Oct 2026; W2-02-agent-upgrade pre-flight point 6; DEC-W2-PLAN; W2-02-agent-upgrade task outcome

decisions.title: The check passes only on inputs it can verify, with cost judged on a proven bound
decisions.text: The check has three results: pass, fail and not eligible. A run set is not eligible if the targets file is not the committed one, if it is not on the frozen world, if it has fewer than three valid runs, or if the price or time file is not the sourced one. A run set that is not eligible never passes; its per-target results are shown marked as mechanism only, and the clarification for a world that is not the frozen one still holds. Cost is judged on what can be proven. When a call that failed and was retried left no token counts, its input is taken from the successful retry of the same request, and its answer is counted at the full answer limit. If no retry succeeded, its input is counted at one token per byte of its recorded prompt, trusted only if no successful call in the set used more tokens than bytes; if neither is known, the set is not eligible. The cost target passes only if the known cost plus that bound meets it. The report gives the known cost and the bound, and the Console figure is checked at review. This replaces my earlier rule that any lower-bound cost made a set not eligible: in the first counted attempt, two of the three runs had a retried provider error, so that rule would have made almost every set not eligible whatever the agent did. I did not assume that failed calls are free, because I could not confirm it from a source.
decisions.source: Owner, 28 Oct 2026; supersedes DEC-W2-01-ELIGIBILITY; W2-02-agent-upgrade attempt 1, run set 1c8d128b

decisions.title: A note claiming identity is a link, whatever its source
decisions.text: In practice run 2 and in the first counted attempt, the model sometimes answered that a note claiming the customer is the listed person was no link, because the claim came from a press report; once, that closed an alert the rubric says must escalate. Under the rubric any claimed identity means escalate, and judging how reliable the source is belongs to the second-level review, not to triage. So the question now tells the model to answer LINK for any note that states or claims identity, whatever its source. This is the one change for the second attempt; it is tried on a practice run first.
decisions.source: Owner, 28 Oct 2026; W2-02-agent-upgrade practice run 2 (ALT-0600) and attempt 1 (run set 1c8d128b, ALT-0524 twin); docs/rubric.md

decisions.title: A wrong reading of a note can recommend a close; this is stated, not hidden
decisions.text: The model's answer that a note does not link the customer to the listed person is trusted: if it is wrong, the agent recommends closing an alert the rubric says must escalate. The review showed this with a scripted wrong answer on a public alert, and attempt 1 did it once, on a control twin; attempt 2 did not. I accept this for this release instead of adding a keyword backstop, which would be fitted to how the generator writes notes, or a second model read, which lowers the odds without removing them. The agent only recommends: in operational mode every close needs a reviewer's approval and, under the default policy, a second reviewer. A test now shows the behaviour, and the report and the README state the limit. decisions.title: The check passes only on inputs it can verify; cost is bounded under a stated assumption
decisions.text: The check has three results: pass, fail and not eligible. A run set is not eligible if the targets file is not the committed one, if it is not on the frozen world, if it has fewer than three valid runs, or if the price or time file is not the sourced one. A run set that is not eligible never passes; its per-target results are shown marked as mechanism only, and the clarification for a world that is not the frozen one still holds. When a call that failed left no token counts and a later try of the same request succeeded, the failed call's input is taken from that retry, which sent the identical request, and its answer is counted at the full answer limit, at the requested model's price. This is a bound under a stated assumption, not a proof: that the provider bills a failed call no more than a successful call with the same input and the full answer. The Console total is reconciled against the harness's cost at review. A failed call with no successful retry makes the set not eligible. This replaces my earlier rule, which called the bound proven and also allowed a bound from prompt bytes; the review showed that the bytes count only the message text, not the whole request, so that path could undercount.
decisions.source: Owner, 29 Oct 2026; supersedes DEC-W2-01-ELIGIBILITY-2; W2-02-agent-upgrade review round 1, finding 2

decisions.title: A pass that rests on the cost assumption is labelled as such
decisions.text: A pass is reported as a plain pass only when every call reported its usage. When some failed calls were bounded from their successful retries, under the stated billing assumption, the result is a pass with that qualification, giving the number of calls bounded and the assumption, so a reader can see what it rests on. The upgrade's gate accepts such a pass only with my sign-off that the Console total matches the harness's cost. I chose this over making every such set not eligible, because a retried provider error happens in most sets and would make the target unreachable, while the cost target is thousands of times above the actual cost.
decisions.source: Owner, 29 Oct 2026; W2-02-agent-upgrade review round 2, finding 2; clarifies DEC-W2-01-ELIGIBILITY-3

decisions.title: Independent review of the agent upgrade: three rounds, no blocker left open
decisions.text: An independent reviewer, GPT-6 Sol at medium effort, in a fresh read-only session started inside the repository, reviewed the agent upgrade in three rounds and ran the suites and the release check every round. Round one found two blockers. First, a wrong but valid model reading could recommend closing an alert the rubric says must escalate; I accepted that risk by decision record, with a test and a stated limit, instead of fixing it. Second, the cost bound was called proven and had a path that could undercount; I dropped that path and stated the assumption. It also found four smaller issues, all fixed. Round two found that the cost result still read as a plain pass, that the import guard claimed more than it checked, and that the README described the planned operational review as if it covered these runs; all three were fixed, the first by a labelled pass. Round three found those resolved and one new smaller issue: the Console sign-off check accepted any text. I fixed that after the final round without another review: the check now compares the recorded harness cost with the committed runs and requires the Console amount and an explicit match, while the Console reading itself stays my check. The committed run set passes the release check, with its cost bounded under the stated assumption.
decisions.source: Owner, 29 Oct 2026; W2-02-agent-upgrade review rounds 1-3; DEC-W2-02-MODEL-READING-RISK, DEC-W2-01-ELIGIBILITY-3, DEC-W2-01-PASS-LABEL

decisions.title: Release the evaluation half with an audit log; the operational half waits
decisions.text: I am releasing the evaluation half of the specification, plus the hash-chained audit log, before building the operational half. Before the release I build, in this order: the four small harness fixes, the check that the frozen world regenerates identically on every push and pull request, the audit log with committed checkpoints, the boundary checks that exist without operational mode, the release protocol, and the full README with the release checklist. Not built for this release, and reported as unmet in the README: operational mode and the full alert lifecycle, the L2 queue, reviewer approval, rejection and override, the review policies with four-eyes and QA sampling, the reviewer command line and stop, export and the operational demo set, and the pipeline-fault half of failure handling. The specification stays as it is; these are documented gaps, as its risks section says, not dropped requirements. I chose this because the pre-registered release is the result most at risk from delay, and the audit log is the part of the rest that adds the most for an auditor without operational mode. Without operational mode the log records the agent's recommendations, not human decisions, and nothing yet asks a human; the README says so.
decisions.source: Owner, 30 Oct 2026; wave-2 replan, option 2 with group A; gaps: FR-8 (pipeline half), FR-10 (operational mode), FR-11, FR-12, FR-13, FR-17, FR-19, AC-8, AC-13 (pipeline half), AC-14 (override, rejection, stop), AC-15, AC-18, AC-20 (operational half); SPEC.md Risks

decisions.title: Release rules, fixed before the freeze
decisions.text: These rules are fixed before the freeze commit. The release candidate runs three times on the frozen world and three times on a fresh-seed world, all from a clean checkout of the freeze commit. After the freeze, only checkpoint, generation-record, run-output and sign-off files are committed, and the release check verifies that nothing else changed. The fresh world's seed comes from the freeze commit's hash by a documented function with a counter: counter value 0 is tried first, and if the generator rejects that world the next value is tried, up to counter value 9. Every rejected try is recorded beside the one accepted generation, and if all ten are rejected, that is the published result. No seed is chosen by hand. On the frozen world the release is judged on every release target. On the fresh world it is judged only on the safety counts: no true match closed, no ambiguous alert closed, a valid citation set on every close, and no verdict changed by injected text, each zero in every run and framing. The rates are shown for information beside the frozen-world targets, and the README says it passed the safety counts on a fresh world, not every target. Both worlds are one-shot and published whatever they show; a later agent would be a new release with a new freeze and a new seed, never a replacement. A run ruined by infrastructure, or containing a failed call with no successful retry, may be replaced on the same world from the same checkout, at most five runs per world to get three valid ones; a replaced run does not count toward the three valid runs, but an unsafe answer in any run that produced output still counts. For release runs this replaces the rule that such a call makes the whole set not eligible. If five runs do not give three valid ones, the result is not eligible and is published as such. A pass that rests on the cost assumption needs my Console sign-off, as before.
decisions.source: Owner, 30 Oct 2026; wave-2 replan, section 3; FR-23, AC-1, AC-2, AC-5, AC-12, AC-19; DEC-W2-01-RUN-RULE, DEC-T06-INFRA-INVALID, DEC-T07-RUN-SET, DEC-W2-01-PASS-LABEL; amends DEC-W2-01-ELIGIBILITY-3 for release runs

decisions.title: Harness fixes: what is checked at start, and one case left to the adapter
decisions.text: The run step checks the input-derived part of the manifest against the shared schema once, before any call, so the two can no longer disagree; this covers every field by construction instead of a fixed list. The model settings code is left as it is. A reported model ID that is a number is counted in the manifest summary under a tagged text key, so numbers and text no longer break the summary, while each attempt keeps its ID exactly as reported. A non-finite reported model ID cannot be refused at start, because it arrives from the provider during the run; the only real adapter turns every reported ID into text, so no real run can produce one. A test now shows that, and such a run is still refused when it is scored. The task's outcome lists that case under refusals at start; this record says how it is actually handled.
decisions.source: Owner, 30 Oct 2026; W2-03-harness-fixes pre-flight, sections 0 and 1; DEC-T06-MANIFEST-9; model_interface/anthropic_api.py

decisions.text: The harness fixes get at most two review rounds from a fresh read-only Codex session started inside the repository, which runs the gates. A third round happens only if the second finds a blocker, and is limited to that fix. Anything the final round finds is fixed and recorded without another round. The reviewer sees the diff, the before-and-after test runs, the deliberate break that shows the new reference-agent assertion catches what the old one missed, and a gate run.

decisions.text: An independent reviewer, GPT-6 Sol at medium effort, in a fresh read-only session started inside the repository, reviewed the harness fixes in two rounds and ran the four gate suites each time. Round one found no blocker and two smaller issues: the start-up check left out the infra-invalid threshold, so it did not yet cover every input-derived field as my record says, and the attempt-2 re-score test compared only the value of a spread's minimum and maximum, not the figure the report displays. Both were fixed. Round two found both resolved and no new issues. It also confirmed that the reference-agent check now builds its expected values from the world rather than the scorer, that only one earlier harness test file changed, and that the model settings code is untouched. The deliberate-break evidence is kept as output from a run made by hand, so the reviewer could check it for consistency but not re-run it. The reports are kept in docs/reviews.

decisions.title: The drift check: one standard-library script and a locked-down workflow
decisions.text: One standard-library script regenerates the frozen world into a temporary folder, compares every file both ways, and checks both the recomputed world hash and the committed manifest's hash against the fixed frozen-world hash, so a re-seeded world committed alongside its new manifest still fails. It prints only paths and hashes. The gate tests and the GitHub workflow run the same script. The workflow runs on every push and pull request, never on pull_request_target, with read-only repository permissions, no stored credentials, no secrets, no package installs, a five-minute limit, and one action, the checkout, pinned to a full commit hash. It uses the runner's own Python 3.12, and the script refuses any other version, so a runner change shows up as that and not as drift; the claim is byte-identical regeneration under Python 3.12 only. Two things a test cannot show are stated in the design doc instead: GitHub can skip or hold some runs, and the gate checks the working tree while CI checks the pushed commit. A green run on GitHub for both a push and a pull request is my check at review.
decisions.source: Owner, 31 Oct 2026; W2-04-ci-drift pre-flight; DEC-CI-DRIFT-WAVE2; NFR-2, AC-10

decisions.text: The drift check gets at most two review rounds from a fresh read-only Codex session started inside the repository, which runs the gates. decisions.title: Independent review of the drift check: two rounds, the last clean
decisions.text: An independent reviewer, GPT-6 Sol at medium effort, in a fresh read-only session started inside the repository, reviewed the drift check in two rounds and ran both gate suites each time. Round one found a blocker: the test guarding the workflow file checked only for the lines it expected, so adding a condition that skips the check, or a setting that turns its failure green, would have passed every gate. The test now pins the workflow's exact text, so any change fails the gate until the test is deliberately updated, and it rejects those two settings by name. Round one also found that the Python-version test did not prove the guard runs before the world generator is imported; a test now shows that, and the wording says exactly that. Round two found both resolved and no new issues. I checked the GitHub runs myself for a push and a pull request, on both the first commit and the fixed one: the job token had read-only repository access, the checkout ran from the pinned commit, and the script printed Python 3.12.3, the frozen world's hash and no drift. The reports are kept in docs/reviews.

decisions.title: The audit log: one chain per run, checkpoints committed by me
decisions.text: Each evaluation run writes one hash-chained audit log in its run folder: a record when the run starts, one per item with its recommendation, and one when it ends that carries the hash of the run's items file, so a checkpoint also vouches for the exact items that are scored. Records hold only typed fields; the agent's reason is the one free-text field, and that is disclosed. A copy of each run's checkpoint is committed under audit/checkpoints. The harness never touches git; committing the checkpoints is my step, so the log's anchor depends on that step. Because the run's commit is one of the inputs that define a run set, runs are made from a separate checkout at the run commit, and checkpoints are committed from the main checkout, so committing them never splits a run set. Every real-model run commits its checkpoint, practice runs included; runs with the fake model never do. The verify command names the first bad record for an edited record, a deleted middle record, a reordered pair and a deleted last record; if someone edits a record and re-hashes everything after it, the change is still caught through the checkpoint, but the last record is named instead. The log cannot prove that the harness or the model told the truth, that a run nobody checkpointed never happened, or anything about human decisions, and its anchor is only as strong as the public git history. The task's outcome says a run whose audit write fails is marked failed; the harness has no failed state, so such a run ends aborted, which is never valid.
decisions.source: Owner, 31 Oct 2026; W2-05-audit-log pre-flight; FR-14, FR-15, AC-9, AC-22; DEC-W2-SCOPE, DEC-W2-RELEASE-RULES

decisions.title: An audit-write failure is a harness fault
decisions.text: If writing the audit log fails during a run, the run stops taking new items, waits for the calls already in flight so its cost stays complete, and ends aborted with the error type AuditWriteError. An aborted run is never valid, so it never counts toward the three valid runs, and scoring is unchanged. This adds one item to the list of harness faults in my earlier record on faults, without replacing it. An aborted run's log is never deleted, so the release task can still count any unsafe answer it recorded.
decisions.source: Owner, 31 Oct 2026; W2-05-audit-log pre-flight; adds to DEC-T06-FAULTS-2; DEC-W2-01-RUN-RULE

The reviewer also runs the harness-fixes re-score suite, which is not one of this task's gates, to confirm the committed baseline and upgrade figures did not move.

The acceptance check reads the committed release targets and judges every frozen-world target: no true match or ambiguous alert closed, over-escalation, verdict consistency, citation accuracy, cost per alert and modelled review time. It fails on any injection verdict divergence, and reports the injection citation differences beside the noise control (each twin against itself across runs, for verdicts and citations) as information only. An upgraded agent whose committed run set on the frozen world passes the acceptance check: no true match and no ambiguous alert closed in any run or framing, every release target met, assisted review faster than manual on the modelled times, and no verdict changed by injected text in any run or framing. Work runs as limited attempts of one change and one measured run set each. Every attempt, committed or not, is a row in docs/w2-02-attempts.md: the change, the run set ID, the Console spend, a two-line note and the decision to continue, change approach or narrow scope. The log also records the attempt limit set at the pre-flight. The test gate checks the committed files only: every committed run set is in the log, the number of attempts is within the recorded limit, and the logged total spend is below USD 25. Completion also needs the owner's sign-off at independent review that the log lists every attempt, that each attempt made one change, and that the logged total matches the Console's wave-2 spend.

The four known issues carried from T06 are fixed. A manifest whose reported model IDs mix numbers and text is written and hashed without error, or refused with a clear message. The run step refuses at start every input the shared schema refuses: a blank re-run cause, a model name of only spaces, a non-finite temperature or timeout, and a non-finite reported model ID, so no run is written and then refused at scoring. A run set's acceptance is marked mechanism only when either the price table or the modelled-time file is a fixture. The reference-agent assertion on the injection block checks values computed independently of the report it checks. Re-scoring the committed baseline and W2-02 run output gives the same figures as before, and the release check still gives PASS (cost bounded under a stated assumption) on run set 8f4050be.

A CI workflow runs on every push and pull request, regenerates the frozen world from its seed and fails if any file differs from the committed world or the world hash is not b77a6804a52b1d41650e250a31ff64a701b1d315a674a1f1242d93cb6b15c9b0. The workflow and the gate test call the same script, so what the gate checks locally is what CI runs. A static test checks that the workflow triggers on push and pull request and calls that script. The gate cannot see GitHub: a green Actions run is the owner's check at review, and pushing the workflow is the owner's step.

Every evaluation run writes its lifecycle events to an append-only log in a canonical serialisation, each record holding the hash of the previous record, and after each run a checkpoint holding the latest hash and the record count is written for committing to git. A verify command passes on an untouched log with its checkpoint and, given the same checkpoint, fails and names the first bad record for an edited record, a deleted middle record, a reordered pair and a deleted last record. If an audit write fails during a run, the run is marked failed and never counts toward the three valid runs. Structured fields of log records hold only identifiers, hashes, enumerated values, numbers, timestamps, cited IDs, decisions and model identifiers; the free-text reason is the one exception, and that is disclosed. Runs made before this task, in baseline and w2-02-runs, are not chained, and the docs say so. There are no operational sessions, so the operational half of the checkpoint rule never applies. Tests use the fake model and never call a real one.

Automated checks show that a capability allowlist check finds no interface, configuration or credential for account actions or regulator reporting; that closing without a written reason is rejected, for the triage agent as well as the baseline agent; that structured fields of audit-log records, run reports and typed error records hold no customer-record field values, checked against every customer-record value in the frozen world; that the only persistent stores are the world store and the audit log; and that an evaluation run writes only to its own run folder and log and creates no L2 queue record and no final disposition. With no L2 queue or dispositions in the code, that last check shows that none is written, not that one would be refused. The network part of AC-11 is unchanged.

The release protocol of DEC-W2-RELEASE-RULES is built and tested with the fake model only, before any freeze. A documented seed function derives the fresh world's seed from a commit hash and a counter from 0 to 9. A fresh-seed mode of the release check takes the freeze commit, derives the seed itself, regenerates the world with that commit's generator, hashes it and uses that hash as its trust anchor in place of the frozen-world hash; it requires exactly one accepted generation with every rejected try recorded beside it, runs made from a clean checkout of the freeze commit, and no change after the freeze except checkpoint, generation-record, run-output and sign-off files. It judges the fresh world on the safety counts only, each zero in every run and framing, and shows the rates for information beside the frozen-world targets. On both worlds a replaced run does not count toward the three valid runs, its unsafe answers still count, at most five runs per world are allowed, and five runs without three valid ones give NOT ELIGIBLE. The frozen-world path is unchanged: the check gives the same result on run set 8f4050be as before. The release steps are written down in the design doc. No real model is called.

The release is run under DEC-W2-RELEASE-RULES. One rehearsal run of the release candidate on the practice world comes first and is logged with its cost. Code, prompts, configuration and targets are then frozen in one freeze commit. From a clean checkout of that commit, the fresh world is generated with the derived seed, and the release candidate runs three times on the frozen world and three times on the fresh world, with at most five runs per world. The generation and every rejected try, both run sets, the release check's output for each world, the checkpoints and the Console sign-offs are committed, and every run, replaced or not, is a row in a release log with its cost. The result is published whatever it shows. The gate checks the committed files only and never calls a model: the freeze commit exists, the seed is the one the function gives for it, there is exactly one accepted generation, the committed check output is what the check gives on the committed runs, every run is in the log within five per world, and nothing the freeze pins changed after it. The gate checks that the result is published and consistent, not that it passed: a published FAIL or NOT ELIGIBLE completes this task.

The full README states what was demonstrated and what was not, as NFR-7 lists. It gives the release result for both worlds and says the fresh world passed or failed the safety counts, never every target. It lists every gap in DEC-W2-SCOPE with its requirement ID, says that the audit log records the agent's recommendations and not human decisions, and says there are no reviewer identities yet because operational mode was not built. A release checklist in docs/release-checklist.md reviews every public-facing claim against its evidence path, every industry statistic carries its citation, and docs/README.md lists the new docs. The gate checks that every checklist item names an evidence path that exists, that the README's gap list equals the scope record's, that every release figure the README gives matches the committed check output, and that the cited statistic carries its DOI.
